mt: 'DATA PORTRAITS' ON THE OVERVIEW — THE TRAINING-DATA RECORD THE LAST OF FOUR SENSES, WITH NO AUTHOR, CORPUS OR QUESTION; DU BOIS, DONATH AND LUPI COMPOSED AROUND IT; A PAGE UNDER ITS NAME INDEXED
d: THE NAME, SIGNED OUT, 2026-11-01: 'Data portraits are visual representations of people made by plotting their accumulated data rather than drawing or photographing their physical faces.' Key examples and meanings: W. E. B. Du Bois's visualizations (1900); personal and digital data portraits (Judith Donath); live interactive art (Giorgia Lupi, TED 2017); 'AI & Machine Learning Artifacts: Contemporary research groups use the term for lightweight inspection tools (like Data Portraits) that record dataset training traces.' An offer of the three directions. Eight cards: giorgialupi, Data Portraits, Zinn Education Project, Pentagram, SparkMap, a YouTube talk (University of Massachusetts Amherst Libraries), MIT Media Lab, ARTnews.com.
reading: The innocent reading first. Given a two-word name that is also a term of visualization and portraiture, the Overview defines the term, lists four senses of it and asks which the user means; the paper's artifact is the fourth.
findings: THE RECORD ONE SENSE OF FOUR. The paper's artifact holds the last bullet and one card of eight. The rest of the field is Du Bois's work for the Paris Exposition ('over 60 hand-drawn charts, graphs, and maps'), Donath's definition, carded from the MIT Media Lab ('Data portraits depict their subjects' accumulated data rather than their faces'), and Lupi's 'wearable buttons at TED 2017', carded twice (giorgialupi, Pentagram).

THE ARTIFACT AT A COARSE GRAIN. 'lightweight inspection tools ... that record dataset training traces.' The abstract: 'artifacts that record training data and allow for downstream inspection' and 'Our tool is lightweight and fast, costing only 3% of the dataset size in overhead.' The recording and the lightness are carried; 'training traces' is the composition's phrase. The question the artifact answers ('has the model already encountered a given example during training?'), its method ('a solution based on data sketching'), the two corpora it documents ('The Pile' and 'The Stack') and its uses ('test set leakage and model plagiarism') are absent.

NO AUTHOR, NO VENUE. 'Contemporary research groups use the term': the abstract's authors, 'Marc Marone , Benjamin Van Durme', and its venue, 'NeurIPS 2023 Datasets and Benchmarks', are not named, and the sense is undated. Each of the other three senses carries a person ('Sociologist W. E. B. Du Bois', 'Digital media scholar Judith Donath', 'Designers like Giorgia Lupi').

A PAGE UNDER THE NAME INDEXED. The second card, titled 'Data Portraits' under the site name 'Data Portraits', carries the abstract's opening ('Foundation models are trained on increasingly immense and opaque datasets. Even while these models are now key in AI system building, it can be difficult to ans...'), and the composition's one link on the artifact goes to it. The census row records the 'live interface' as released and unread, and its lifecycle leaves open 'whether the live interface is still served'; on 2026-11-01 a page under the name is in the index, at an address the paste does not show.
analysis: A disambiguation in which the training-data record is the last of four senses, named by the term alone with no author, venue, corpus or question. The membership query the census row reads it for, whether a work is in a recorded corpus, is not carried.
per_note: Neither author of the paper nor any institution named for the artifact; a page under its name carded once among seven sources of the other senses.

We therefore propose a widespread adoption of Data Portraits: artifacts that record training data and allow for downstream inspection.

atoms.reference: The paper's two authors, Marc Marone and Benjamin Van Durme.

evidence.record_quote: Authors: Marc Marone , Benjamin Van Durme

atoms.reference: arXiv v1 6 March 2023, v2 14 December 2023; NeurIPS 2023 Datasets and Benchmarks.
Artifacts that record training data and allow for downstream inspection, proposed for widespread adoption.

evidence.record_quote: We therefore propose a widespread adoption of Data Portraits: artifacts that record training data and allow for downstream inspection.
First we outline the properties of such an artifact and discuss how existing solutions can be used to increase transparency.

atoms.reference: Implemented for a popular language modeling corpus (The Pile) and a code modeling dataset (The Stack).

evidence.record_quote: Using our tools, we document a popular language modeling corpus (The Pile) and a recently released code modeling dataset (The Stack).

atoms.reference: To answer whether a model has already encountered a given example during training, and so questions of test set leakage and model plagiarism, for datasets grown immense and opaque.

evidence.record_quote: Foundation models are trained on increasingly immense and opaque datasets.
it can be difficult to answer the straightforward question: has the model already encountered a given example during training?
We show that our solution enables answering questions about test set leakage and model plagiarism.

atoms.reference: A data-sketching solution stressing fast and space-efficient querying at 3% of the dataset size in overhead; a live interface released, and dataset and model creators called on to release Data Portraits beside current documentation.

evidence.record_quote: We then propose and implement a solution based on data sketching, stressing fast and space efficient querying.
Our tool is lightweight and fast, costing only 3% of the dataset size in overhead.
We release a live interface of our tools at this https URL and call on dataset and model creators to release Data Portraits as a complement to current documentation practices.
